title: The Millet Comeback: How India's Ancient Supergrain Is Conquering American Menus and NRI Kitchens
excerpt: From Silicon Valley dosa joints to Whole Foods shelves, millets are having their mainstream moment — and the Indian diaspora is leading the charge.
body:
There is a quiet revolution happening in Indian kitchens across America. The grain that your grandmother dismissed as "poor people's food" is now showing up on DoorDash menus with words like "artisanal," "gluten-free," and "ancient." Millets — ragi, bajra, jowar, and their nutritionally dense cousins — are having their mainstream moment. And for NRIs navigating the intersection of health consciousness and cultural identity, the timing could not be better.

## From Government Initiative to Global Plate

The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets at India's urging, and the ripple effects are still expanding. India solidified its position as the global leader in millet production in 2024-25, achieving a record 18.59 million tonnes. Domestic sales of millet-based products surged to ₹814 crore through focused Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes. The government's push was not just symbolic — it created the agricultural and industrial infrastructure for millets to scale.

That scale is now reaching American shores. In the Bay Area, restaurants like Indian Crepe Co. serve millet dosas and button idlis made from millet-and-lentil batter, listed on DoorDash alongside South Indian filter coffee. In New York, several Indian restaurants have added millet bowls and ragi roti to their menus. The positioning is deliberate: these are not marketed as Indian health food, but simply as good food that happens to be healthy.

## The Wellness Convergence

Millets' American moment is riding a larger wave. The US wellness market has been obsessed with "ancient grains" for years — quinoa, amaranth, farro — and millets fit the narrative perfectly. They are gluten-free, high in protein and fibre, rich in iron and calcium, and have a lower glycemic index than rice or wheat. For health-conscious NRIs who grew up eating ragi mudde in Karnataka or bajra roti in Rajasthan, the discovery that their childhood staples are now "superfoods" carries a particular irony.

FMCG brands are capitalising aggressively. India's largest brands are leveraging organic millet agriculture to build smarter product portfolios — millet cookies, millet-based ready-to-eat meals, and millet snack bars designed for both the Indian domestic market and export. The playbook mirrors how turmeric went from kitchen spice to wellness supplement: start with authenticity, add scientific credibility, and let health-conscious consumers do the rest.

## The Cultural Reclamation

For many in the Indian diaspora, the millet trend carries deeper resonance than a simple health food story. Millets were India's staple grains for millennia before the Green Revolution of the 1960s shifted production toward rice and wheat. In that transition, millets lost their prestige. They became associated with poverty, with rural backwardness, with the food your family ate before they "made it."

The reversal of that narrative — millets as premium, aspirational, modern — is a form of cultural reclamation. When a second-generation Indian American orders a ragi dosa at a trendy Bay Area restaurant and pays $14 for it, they are not just buying breakfast. They are reconnecting with a food tradition that their parents' generation was encouraged to leave behind.

## Challenges on the Path

The millet mainstreaming faces real obstacles. Taste remains a barrier: millets have a distinct, earthy flavour that does not universally appeal, especially to palates raised on refined flour and white rice. Cooking with millets requires different techniques and knowledge that many NRI home cooks lack. And pricing in the US remains high — organic millet flour can cost three to four times more than regular wheat flour.

Supply chain logistics also complicate matters. While India produces vast quantities, the infrastructure for processing, packaging, and exporting millets to meet US food safety standards is still developing. Many of the millet products available at Indian grocery stores in America are imported from small Indian companies with limited quality control.

## What's Next

The trajectory is clear, even if the pace is uncertain. As India's millet production infrastructure matures and US consumer awareness grows, millets are positioned to follow the path of other Indian exports that went from niche to mainstream — think turmeric, ghee, and chai. For the diaspora, the millet revolution offers something rare: a trend where being Indian is not just relevant but central to the story.

The grain your grandmother served without fanfare is now a global superfood. She would probably shrug and say she knew all along.
author: Diaspora Desk
